statement: In the world's population in 2020, alcohol drinking compared with a counterfactual in which no one had ever drunk (lifetime abstention) is estimated by one modelling study to account for 741,300 new cancer cases (95% uncertainty interval 558,500–951,200), about 4 in every 100 new cancers (4.1%, 3.1%–5.3%; non-melanoma skin cancer excluded): about 6 in 100 new cancers in men (568,700 cases; 6.1%) and 2 in 100 in women (172,600; 2.0%) (Rumgay et al., 2021; no funding, no competing interests declared). The model counts only the cancers that the International Agency for Research on Cancer judges to be caused by alcohol: oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only) 189,700 cases, 31.6% of all oesophageal cancers; liver (hepatocellular carcinoma only) 154,700, 17.3%; female breast 98,300, 4.4%; colon 91,500, 8.1%; lip and oral cavity 74,900, 20.2%; rectum 65,100, 9.0%; pharynx 39,400, 22.0%; and larynx 27,600, 15.0%. It attributes 346,400 cases (46.7%) to drinking more than 60 g of ethanol a day, 291,800 (39.4%) to 20–60 g and 103,100 (13.9%; interval 82,600–207,200) to less than 20 g a day (up to about two drinks), including 41,300 (35,400–145,800) to drinking up to 10 g a day, of which 24,600 were in women, 14.3% of women's alcohol-attributed cancers. These are model estimates, not counts of people whose cancer was traced to drinking: they combine drinking estimated from 2010 sales and surveys, assumed to act 10 years later, with relative-risk curves for current drinking from World Cancer Research Fund reviews of observational studies, applied in the same way to every country; former drinkers carry no extra risk in the main analysis; the uncertainty intervals carry only the uncertainty in drinking and in the relative risks, leave out that in cancer incidence, the 10-year delay and the model's structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures; and the hepatocellular share behind the liver figure comes from unpublished estimates. Adding stomach and pancreatic cancer raised the total to 808,700, and counting former drinking raised it to 925,900, though the increment the paper gives for this (135,000) does not match its own totals. Earlier global estimates cited by the paper, for other years and with other choices, were 5.5% of new cancers in 2012 and 4.8% to 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019; an earlier model by an overlapping team estimated 487 thousand cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004 (377 thousand in men, 111 thousand in women; no uncertainty intervals; Rehm et al., 2009); and in the Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, cancers made up 27.1% of the deaths attributed to alcohol in women aged 50 and older and 18.9% in men (Griswold et al., 2018). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: A model estimated that about 741,000 new cancers worldwide in 2020, about 4 in every 100 new cancers, were caused by drinking, compared with a world where no one had ever drunk: about 6 in 100 new cancers in men and 2 in 100 in women. Gullet, liver, breast, bowel and mouth cancers made up most of them. Most were linked to drinking more than 20 g of alcohol a day (about two drinks); about 103,000 were linked to less than that, and about 41,000 to up to 10 g a day, more than half of these in women. These are computer estimates, not counted cases: they take cancer risks from studies of groups of people and apply them to every country, and some of the model's choices are uncertain. An older model by an overlapping team estimated 487,000 cancer deaths caused by alcohol in 2004.
population: The world's population in 2020 (exposure modelled for ages 15 and over), all countries in GLOBOCAN 2020; for comparison, the world's population in 2004 and in 2016
exposure: Current drinking, estimated from 2010 adult per-capita consumption (recorded, unrecorded and tourist) and surveys, with intake among current drinkers modelled from 0.1 to 150 g of ethanol a day; categories below 20 g, 20–60 g and above 60 g a day
comparator: A counterfactual of lifetime abstention for everyone (theoretical minimum-risk exposure); no alcohol consumption in the 2004 model
outcome: New cancer cases in 2020 (GLOBOCAN 2020) at the sites with sufficient evidence of causation by alcohol in IARC monograph 100E: lip and oral cavity, pharynx, oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma), colon, rectum, liver (hepatocellular carcinoma), larynx and female breast; for comparison, cancer deaths in 2004 (WHO comparative risk assessment) and the cancer share of alcohol-attributable deaths in 2016 (Global Burden of Disease)

evidence.extracted: Limitations stated by the authors: the under-reporting correction does not vary by age or sex and ignores changes before and after 2010; surveys underestimate former drinking; data quality varies by country; residual confounding by tobacco and no modelling of synergy with tobacco, hepatitis B or C, aflatoxin or obesity; no population-specific relative risks; 2020 incidence not adjusted for COVID-19 disruptions.

risk_of_bias.note: The estimate takes the relative-risk curves as causal and unbiased; they come from observational studies with the confounding, under-reporting and reference-group problems set out in the answer on which cancers (low certainty there, very low for light drinking); the World Cancer Research Fund curves used are in an appendix that was not read, and their reference group is not stated in the main text (card sc_rumgay_2021).

inconsistency.note: Earlier global estimates cited by the paper (5.5% of new cancers in 2012; 4.8% and 4.9% of cancer deaths in 2016 and 2019) are of similar size, though they share inputs; the 2004 death estimate measures a different outcome.

indirectness.note: One set of relative risks, mainly from cohorts in high-income countries, applied to every population; exposure from 2010 per-capita consumption and surveys, with under-reporting corrected in one way for all ages and both sexes and a fixed 10-year delay; current drinking only; ten countries imputed from their region; GLOBOCAN incidence itself modelled for many countries.

imprecision.note: The intervals leave out uncertainty in incidence, histological splits, latency and model structure, and are lopsided for the low-intake figures (103,100, 82,600–207,200; 41,300, 35,400–145,800); the 2004 estimate has no intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a model; publication bias in the studies behind the curves is covered under risk of bias.

grade.reasoning: Model estimates are not graded as evidence of an effect: the claim describes what the models estimate (relation describes), and its certainty comes from the evidence behind the relative-risk curves (observational, low at best), rated down for the model's indirectness and for its incomplete uncertainty intervals, which gives very low. No upgrade applies to a modelled count. Status replicated by the same team: the 2020 case estimate and the 2004 death estimate come from overlapping authors, the same comparative-risk-assessment method and WHO exposure data; the Global Burden of Disease figure is a share of deaths from a different group drawing on overlapping studies, and is not counted as independent.
